tagline: Two roads follow the Hudson, above the cliffs and below
intro: The Palisades Scenic Byway offers two levels of travel along the Hudson: the Palisades Interstate Parkway on the cliff tops and Henry Hudson Drive between the cliffs and river. New Jersey designated the route in 2005; NJDOT identifies its historic and scenic qualities and describes the parkway as a road designed within a park. The Federal Highway Administration also lists it as a National Scenic Byway, emphasizing its connection from metropolitan New York to protected parkland.

Quarrying threatened the Palisades when New York and New Jersey began acquiring land for protection in 1900. Henry Hudson Drive was built between 1912 and 1940 to reach the riverfront. John D. Rockefeller’s 1933 gift of 700 acres helped advance a parkway above it, but opposition from the New Jersey Highway Commission stalled the plan. Robert Moses worked on the parkway’s design, with landscape architects and engineers chosen to develop the road. The New Jersey section was completed in 1957.

Travel south from the state-line end toward Fort Lee and the George Washington Bridge. State Line Lookout occupies the highest point of the cliffs, 532 feet. At Alpine, the riverfront excursion reaches Kearney House. Finish at Fort Lee Historic Park, whose bluff-top overlooks face the bridge, Hudson River and Upper Manhattan.

moments.title: State Line Lookout
moments.text: State Line Lookout stands at the highest point of the Palisades cliffs, 532 feet. It is one of three overlooks reached from the parkway, alongside Alpine and Rockefeller lookouts. NJDOT describes views of the Palisades, Hudson River and New York City skyline from the byway’s upper and lower roads. That relationship between driving and looking was deliberate: the parkway’s designers sought a scenic driving experience while limiting effects on the park’s natural environment. The park’s founding mission was to protect these cliffs for future generations, a purpose its byway plan continues to recognize.

moments.title: Kearney House, Alpine
moments.text: This stone house at Closter Landing changed from family home to tavern and later to a park police station. James and Rachel Kearney purchased it in 1817. After James died in 1831, Rachel used the house as a tavern, and the building was expanded for that business. The Palisades Interstate Park Commission bought it in 1907 and used it as a police station in the 1920s. The park now uses it as the Kearney House museum. In 1936, the Historic American Buildings Survey documented it under the name Cornwallis Headquarters, an association modern historians dispute.

moments.title: Fort Lee Historic Park
moments.text: The blockhouse, battery and quarters here reconstruct George Washington’s 1776 encampment on the bluff above Burdett’s Landing. Construction of the original fort began in July 1776, after Washington ordered General Mercer to gather troops and fortify the west bank of the Hudson. Together with Fort Washington across the river, it was intended to defend the lower Hudson against British warships. Washington and Nathanael Greene ordered the fort evacuated on the morning of November 20, 1776, after the loss of Fort Washington across the river. At the park’s north end, two overlooks face the George Washington Bridge, the Hudson and Upper Manhattan.
moments.notice: The blockhouse and battery are reconstructions of the Revolutionary War encampment.

practical: State Line Lookout: Commercial vehicles are prohibited on the entire Palisades Interstate Parkway. (checked 2026-10-11)

Kearney House, Alpine: Henry Hudson Drive has seasonal motor-vehicle closures. The archived park advisory places the Dyckman Hill–Alpine Approach section’s winter closure approximately December through April. (checked 2026-10-11)
